question.leadin: This province's sovereignty movement grew stronger during its "Quiet Revolution."
question.text: Name this largest Canadian province, the only majority French-speaking one.
question.clue: During the Great Darkness, conservative policies were enacted in this region by Maurice Duplessis ("du-pleh-SEE") prior to the liberalization of this region during the Quiet Revolution.

swap.text: Although not a province, this Canadian territory is the newest, having been created in 1999 as a territory for the Inuit peoples.
swap.clue: In 1999, this large territory became a separate territory from the Northwest Territories.

question.leadin: This modern day province had its capital at Annapolis Royal until 1749.
question.text: Name this maritime province that was formerly known as Arcadia and that has its capital at Halifax.
question.clue: The 1995 Peace Prize was awarded to the conferences named for this province's village of Pugwash.

swap.leadin: This modern-day province, and Quebec, made up the Province of Canada.
swap.text: Name this Canadian province which makes up modern-day Upper Canada. Ottawa and Toronto are in this province.
swap.clue: The First Nations leader Tecumseh was killed in this province during the Battle of the Thames (TIMS) in the War of 1812.

question.leadin: During this man's tenure, his government created universal health care, as well as the Maple Leaf flag.
question.text: Name this Prime Minister who preceded Pierre Trudeau and won the nobel peace prize for his role in resolving the Suez Crisis.
question.clue: This politician claimed "Canadians do not need to be liberated" in response to the "Vive le Quebec Libre" speech another man gave at Expo 67.

swap.leadin: This man and Gabriel Dumont lost the battle of Batoche during the North-West rebellion.
swap.text: Name this man, who led one rebellion that was ended by the Wolseley expedition and named for this man's settlement at Red River.
swap.clue: This man was captured with the Cree Chief Poundmaker during the Battle of Batoche, and he appointed a tribunal which sentenced Thomas Scott to death.

question.leadin: Answer the following about mass hysterias in history, none of which involve Pumpkin Spice Lattes.
question.text: In 1938, unsubstantiated reports of a "slasher" paralyzed a British town of this name. Another city of this name was leveled in 1917 by a massive ship explosion and provides Boston a Christmas tree every year as thanks for its subsequent aid.
question.clue: During the French and Indian War, the British army kept prisoners on Georges Island in this city's harbor.

swap.text: Both Anthony Eden and his successor Harold Macmillan were members of this British political party. Notable Hitler-appeaser Neville Chamberlain was also a member of this party.
swap.clue: A foreign secretary from this party issued a statement supporting a "national home" in an Ottoman area.

question.text: He was acquitted of any wrongdoing in the conflict over the Red River Settlement, known as the Seven Oaks Massacre. For fifteen points, name this American-born explorer who followed the 520-mile course of a river now named for him which ends in present-day Vancouver, British Columbia.

swap.leadin: This politician oversaw the passage of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
swap.text: Name this politician who ran on the notion of a "Just Society" in one election, and lost power to Joe Clark's Progressive Conservatives for one year.
swap.clue: After the death of Pierre Laporte, this man told reporters "just watch me" following his invocation of the War Measures Act during the October Crisis.

question.leadin: Shortly before his death, this man mused that he wished he had written Gray's "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard."
question.text: Name this British officer who was killed in a 1759 battle that also claimed his French opposite number, the Marquis de Montcalm. He took three musket balls at that battle and was subsequently honored as a British hero.
question.clue: This man's second-in-command, Robert Monckton, was wounded in a battle that paved the way for George Townshend to accept the surrender of a French colonial stronghold.

swap.text: This French explorer of the Gaspe Peninsula and the St. Lawrence River discovered Quebec and Prince Edward Island. He gave Canada its name, claiming it for Francis I in 1534.
swap.clue: On their second voyage, this person made contact with the residents of the village of Stadacona.

question.text: The Thule people, who spread east from Alaska and replaced the Dorset, were the ancestors of this ethnic group which now forms the majority of the populations of Nunavut and Greenland.
question.answerHtml: Inuit [accept Inuk; prompt on (but correct) Eskimo; antiprompt on Kalaallit; antiprompt on Inuktitut; antiprompt on Iñupiaq; do NOT accept or prompt on “Innu” or “Yupik”] (The Innu are a Cree-speaking Algonquian people whose traditional lands confusingly border the southernmost extent of Inuit in Labrador.)
question.clue: In the 1950s, this ethnic group's dogs were killed by the RCMP.

swap.text: This world leader accepted American Bomarc missiles onto his country's soil but only equipped with conventional warheads. He also controversially scrapped the Avro Arrow program.
swap.clue: He also cancelled the Avro Arrow program, halting production of fighter jets in his country, when he signed NORAD with the US. Raised in Saskatchewan, he passed his country's Bill of Rights, and presided over the opening of the St. Lawrence Seaway.

question.leadin: The Sadlermiut were widely hypothesized to be the last remnants of this culture, until genetic studies revealed otherwise.
question.text: Name this culture that preceded the Thule. These people, named after a cape in Nunavut, inhabited much of the Canadian Arctic and Greenland.
question.clue: X-shaped incisions on figures' heads from this culture have been linked to shamanistic travels.

swap.leadin: This party received $700,000 from the Beauharnois Light, Heat, and Power company in exchange for the right to alter the flow of the St. Lawrence River.
swap.text: Name this left-of-center Canadian political party to which Wilfred Laurier and William Lyon Mackenzie King belonged. It is left of the Conservative Party, but right of the New Democratic Party.
swap.answerHtml: Liberal Party of Canada [or Grits; or Parti liberal du Canada]
swap.clue: A request to dissolve parliament by a leader of this party was refused by Governor-General Julian Byng in 1926.

question.leadin: During the Cold War, the governments of Canada and the United States historically operated this defensive line of radar stations.
question.text: Name this line of stations at sites including Point Lay, Alaska and Alert, Nunavut. Either the three-word name or the three-letter acronym they are more commonly known by are acceptable.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about the early history of computation in Canada.
swap.text: The Ferut was used for "backwater calculations" to model the likely effects of this infrastructure project. Prime Minister John Diefenbaker ("DEE-fun-baker") and Queen Elizabeth II ("the-second") attended its opening ceremony in 1959.
swap.answerHtml: St. Lawrence Seaway and Power Project [or Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Seaway System; or la Voie Maritime du Saint-Laurent; prompt on St. Lawrence River; prompt on Welland Canal by asking “What larger project was that a part of?”]
swap.answer: St. Lawrence Seaway and Power Project

question.text: This founder of the Parti Quebecois is considered the spiritual father of the sovereignty movement. Noted for his ubiquitous comb over, he opposed Robert Bourassa, his predecessor in the position of Quebec's premier, during the October Crisis.

swap.leadin: This man passed the Padlock Act to allow the closing of buildings used to propagate "communism," and was slapped with a fine for revoking Frank Roncarelli's liquor license in a landmark supreme court case.
swap.text: Name this leader nicknamed "le Chef," whose government also certified around 20,000 healthy orphans as mentally ill and shipped them to asylums in order to receive federal subsidies.
swap.clue: This Quebecois leader who implemented a set of conservative policies called the Great Darkness before his Union Nationale Party was deposed in 1959.
